title: Welcoming Egyptians who bring true teaching
english: I will address those who have come from Egypt, and it is right to do so. They have gathered here eagerly, with zeal overcoming envy. I mean this Egypt, which a river enriches by raining up out of the earth and spreading wide in its season, to borrow a little, myself, from those who write cleverly about such things. Yet my Christ enriches it still more. He once fled into Egypt, and now he is supplied from Egypt. Then he fled from Herod's murder of the children; now he is given from the fathers' love for their children. He is Christ, the new food for those who hunger well, the greatest food distribution of any ever recorded or believed. He is "the bread that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world" (John 6:33), a life that cannot perish or be destroyed. About him I think I now hear the Father saying, "Out of Egypt I called my Son" (Hosea 11:1).

For "the word has sounded out from you to all people" (1 Thessalonians 1:8), soundly believed and soundly preached. And you are the finest fruit-bearers of all, especially among those who now believe rightly, as far as I know. For I myself, with regard to such food, am not only a lover but also a supplier, and not only a native but already one beyond the border.

For you feed peoples and cities bodily, as far as your kindness reaches. Yet you also feed spiritually, and not some particular people, nor this or that city bounded by small limits, even if they think most splendidly of themselves, but almost the whole world. And you heal, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, for to hunger for these is no great thing and not to hunger for them is easy. You heal "a famine of hearing the word of the Lord" (Amos 8:11). To suffer that famine is most pitiable, and to heal it now is most laborious, "for lawlessness has multiplied" (Matthew 24:12), and I find few genuine healers of it.

Such is your Joseph, the measurer of grain, and ours too, I may say. In surpassing wisdom he knew how to foresee famine, and by prudent stewardship he knew how to heal it with words, using the fine, fattened cows to remedy the ugly, starved ones. Take Joseph in whichever sense you wish: either the lover and maker of immortality, and the one named for it, or his successor in throne and word and grey hair, our new Peter, no less in virtue than in name. By these two men the middle party was cut out and crushed, even if it still writhes in small and weak form, just as the tail does when the snake has been cut through. One of them ended his life in a good old age after many contests and trials, and now watches over our affairs from above, I know well. He stretches out his hand to those who labor for the good, and all the more because he is free from his bonds. The other hastens toward the same lodging, or release, amid the same labors. He already draws near to those above, yet he remains in the flesh just long enough to help the message one last time and to make his journey with richer provisions.

You are the nurslings and bulwarks of these great men, teachers of doctrine and champions and victors for the truth. Neither time nor ruler moved them, neither argument nor envy nor fear, neither accuser nor slanderer, neither open enemy nor secret plotter, neither seeming friend nor stranger. Neither did gold, that hidden tyrant by which now most things are turned and moved as pieces in a game. Neither favors nor threats nor long and repeated exiles moved them, for they could not be caught by confiscation alone, since their great wealth was having nothing. Nothing else, absent or present or expected, lifted them or persuaded them to become worse, to betray anything of the Trinity, and to be deprived of divinity.
orientation: Gregory greets visitors from Egypt as fellow orthodox believers whose confession feeds the church.

title: Egypt's old idols replaced by a faithful people
english: On the contrary, danger only strengthened them, and they grew more zealous in reverence. Suffering for Christ does that: it deepens love, and for great souls it becomes a pledge of the contests still to come. Such are your stories and wonders in our own day, O Egypt.

You once praised to me the goats of Mendes, and Apis of Memphis, a fatted and fleshy calf, and the rites of Isis, and the dismemberments of Osiris, and your august Serapis, a piece of wood worshiped with the help of myth and age and the folly of its worshipers, as if it were some strange and heavenly matter, though matter still, even when falsehood comes to its aid. And there were things more shameful still, manifold images of beasts and creeping things. Christ rose above them all, and so did the preachers of Christ. Others shone in their own ways, each in his own time, and so did the Fathers just now remembered. From them you are known today, O wonderful one, more than all people together are known from all stories at once, old and new.

For this I embrace you and greet you, best of peoples, most loving of Christ, most fervent in reverence, and worthy of your leaders. I have nothing greater to say than this, and no better welcome to offer you. I receive you with a few movements of the tongue and many movements of the mind. You are my people. I call mine all who share the same mind and the same confession, who come from the same Fathers and worship the same Trinity. You are my people. You are mine, even if the envious deny it. And to sting those envious ones still more, see, I offer you the right hand of fellowship before so many witnesses, visible and invisible, and I drive away an old slander with a new kindness. You are my people. You are mine, even though I, the smallest, claim the greatest for my own. Such is the grace of the Spirit: it makes those who share one mind equal in honor. You are my people. You are mine, even from afar, for we are joined in a divine way, in another manner than bodily bulk allows. Bodies are joined by place, but souls are fitted together by the Spirit.

You are my people, who once made it your wisdom to suffer for Christ. Now, if you will listen to me, make it your wisdom not to act, but to count the very power to act as gain enough, and to offer gentleness to Christ as service, just as you once offered endurance. You are the people for whose benefit the Lord has arrayed himself to do good, as he is arrayed to do harm to his enemies. You are the people whom the Lord has chosen for himself out of all those he has called. You are the people painted on the hands of the Lord, to whom the Lord says, "For you are my delight," and, "Your gates are a carving," with all the other promises given afterward to those who are saved. You are my people, and do not wonder at my greed if I keep repeating your name. I delight in speaking it over and over, like those who can never have enough of some sight or sound.

O people of God, and mine as well, your earlier festival was beautiful, the one you held upon the sea, as much as any other delight for the eyes. I watched the sea turned into a forest of masts and covered with a handmade cloud, and saw the beauty of the ships and their speed, as if dispatched for a procession, with a gentle wind set behind the stern like an escort on purpose, convoying a seafaring city to our city. Yet the sight before us now is fairer and more magnificent.
orientation: Gregory contrasts Egypt's former animal and idol cults with the present orthodox Egyptians whom he embraces as his own people.

title: Right tribute to God and the two kinds of beings
english: For you did not cast yourselves in with the many to follow the crowd, nor measure devotion by numbers, nor consent to become a noisy mob rather than a people of God purified by the Word. As was right, you rendered to Caesar the things of Caesar, and you assigned to God the things of God (Matthew 22:21): tribute to the one, reverence to the other (Romans 13:7). After feeding the populace from your own stores, you yourselves have come to be fed by us. For we too hand out food, and a food distribution perhaps no poorer than yours: "Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you" (Proverbs 9:5). With Wisdom I invite you to my table.

I commend your gratitude, and I run to meet your eagerness, because you have put in to us as to your own harbor. You hastened to your like, you honored the kinship of faith, and you judged it absurd that insulters of what is above should agree with one another and fit together, each supposing that what is rotten in him is repaired by their common alliance, like strands made strong by twisting, while you yourselves should fail to come together and be bound to the like-minded, for whom it is far more fitting. For we bring even divinity itself together. So that you may know you have not run to us in vain, nor landed among strangers and outsiders but among your own, well guided by the Spirit, I will speak to you briefly about God. Recognize what is your own, as men recognize their own by the devices on their shields.

I know two highest distinctions among beings: lordship and servitude, not those that tyranny has carved among us or poverty has divided, but those that nature has marked off, if one wishes to call it that. For the first is even beyond nature. The one is productive and ruling and unmoved; the other is made and under authority and subject to change. To say it still more briefly, the one is beyond time, the other is under time. The one is called God, and stands in the three greatest: cause and maker and perfecter, I mean the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. These are neither so detached from one another as to be cut apart by nature, for that is the madness of Arius, nor so contracted as to be confined into one person, for that is the atheism of Sabellius. It is more united than anything wholly divided, and more abundant than anything wholly single. The other order is with us, and is called creation, even if some stand higher than others according to their nearness to God.

This being so, let whoever has his heart toward the Lord come with us, and let us worship the one divinity in the three, bringing no name of lowliness to that unapproachable glory, but always carrying in our throats the exaltations of the one God in the three (Psalms 149:6). For if we cannot properly speak even of greatness of nature, since it is infinite and unbounded, how shall we impose lowliness upon it? But whoever stands estranged from God, and therefore cuts the one being above all beings into an inequality of natures, it will be no wonder if he is cut in two by the sword and his portion is set with the unbelievers (Matthew 24:51), reaping an evil harvest from an evil doctrine, both now and hereafter.
orientation: Gregory praises the Egyptian visitors for true piety and then begins his concise teaching about God and creation.

title: The Son and Spirit share all that the Father has
english: What need is there even to speak about the Father, whom all agree to spare, since they are already possessed by their natural notions of him? He did bear the first dishonor, for he was the first whom the old innovation divided into the Good and the Creator. But about the Son and the Holy Spirit, consider how simply and briefly we will argue. If anyone can show that either of them is changeable or alterable, or measured by time or place or power or activity, or not good by nature, or not self-moving, or not free, or a servant, or a singer of hymns, or afraid, or set free, or not counted together with God, let him prove it, and we will accept it. Then we will be glorified with the dignity of fellow servants, even if we lose God by it.

But if all that the Father has belongs to the Son except causation, and all that belongs to the Son belongs also to the Spirit except sonship and whatever is said of the Son in bodily terms for the sake of my humanity and my salvation, since he took what is mine in order to grant what is his through the new mingling, then stop your raving at last, you sophists of empty words, whose phrases fall flat on the spot. "Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 33:11)—am I to lament you from Scripture?

For my part, I revere the titles of the Word. They are so many, so high and great, that even demons stood in awe of them. I revere the equal honor of the Spirit. I fear the appointed threat against those who blaspheme against him. And blasphemy is not true teaching about God. It is the excluding of the Spirit from divinity. Mark this well: the one blasphemed was the Lord, and the one avenged was the Holy Spirit, clearly as Lord. I cannot bear to be unenlightened after enlightenment, falsifying any of the three into whom I was baptized, and so to be truly buried in the water only to be finished not for new birth but for death.

I dare to utter something, O Trinity, and forgive my recklessness, for the danger concerns the soul. I myself am an image of God, of the glory above, even though I have been set below. I am not convinced to be saved by one of equal honor with myself. If the Holy Spirit is not God, let him first be made God, and then let him make me God, his equal in honor. As it is, what is this trick of grace, or rather of those who give the grace, that I should believe in God and come up without God? That I should confess one thing and be taught another? What thefts and cheats of argument are these, which carry me by one question and confession to something else?

Woe for that brightness, if I am darkened after baptism, if I see those not yet cleansed brighter than I am, if I am gambled away by the false teaching of the one who baptizes me, if I seek a greater Spirit and cannot find him! Give me a second baptism, and think ill of the first. Why do you begrudge me a perfect new birth? Why do you make me, who am a temple of the Spirit as God, into a dwelling place of creation? Why do you honor one part of me and dishonor the other, conducting yourself badly toward divinity, so as to cut the gift away from me, or rather to cut me myself off together with the gift? Either honor the whole, you new theologian, or dishonor the whole, so that even if you are impious you are at least consistent with yourself, and do not judge unequally a nature of equal honor.
orientation: Gregory continues his doctrinal statement, arguing that the Son and Holy Spirit share the full divinity of the Father.

title: Glorify the Trinity with witnesses of Scripture
english: This is the sum of my argument. Glorify with the cherubim, who gather the three holinesses into one lordship and disclose only as much of the first being as their wings open to those who labor with love. Be enlightened with David, who speaks to the Light, "In your light we shall see light" (Psalm 36:9), as seeing the Son in the Spirit. What could shine brighter from afar than this?

Thunder with John, the son of thunder. Sound nothing low about God and nothing earthbound, but only what is high and lifted up. Know him who was in the beginning, and was with God, and was God, the Word (John 1:1), true God from the true Father, not a good fellow slave honored only with the title of Son. Know also the other Comforter (John 14:16), other, that is, than the one who speaks, for the Word belongs to God. When you read, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), see mirrored there the union of being. When you read, "We will come to him and make our dwelling with him" (John 14:23), reckon there the distinction of the persons. When you read the name "of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 28:19), see there the three particular properties.

Be inspired with Luke, and dwell with the Acts of the Apostles. Why do you rank yourself with Ananias and Sapphira, those new embezzlers — if theft of one's own things is truly new? You hold back no silver and no other cheap and small thing, no tongue of gold, no bar of silver, no double coin, as that greedy soldier once did, but you steal divinity itself. You lie, "not to men, but to God" (Acts 5:4), as you have heard. Why do you not even respect the authority of the Spirit, who blows upon whom he wills, and when he wills, and as much as he wills? He visits those with Cornelius before baptism, and others after baptism through the apostles. From both sides, then, the divinity of the Spirit stands attested: from those upon whom he comes as master and not as slave, and from those for whom he is sought for their completion.

Do theology with Paul, who was taken up to the third heaven. At times he counts the three persons together, and he does this with shifting order, not fixed by rank, putting the same one first, next, and last. Why? To declare the equal honor of their nature. At times he names all three, at times only some or one, since what is left out surely follows. At times he gives the activity of God to the Spirit, as making no difference. At times he brings in Christ instead of the Spirit. When he divides the persons, he says, "One God, from whom are all things, and we for him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him" (1 Corinthians 8:6). When he gathers together the one divinity, he says, "For from him, and through him, and to him are all things" (Romans 11:36), that is, through the Holy Spirit, as Scripture shows in many places. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
orientation: Gregory closes the homily by urging his hearers to glorify the Trinity together with the cherubim, David, John, Luke and Paul, and to confess the full divinity of the Spirit.
